Business.title: From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they mean
Business.text:
From the rapidly rising and falling values of Bitcoin to high-profile heists like the hacking of Binance, the world of cryptocurrencies is often in the headlines.

The world's biggest crypto exchange said hackers had gained access to $6.3bn (£4.7bn) worth of digital assets, and while it has frozen about half, many remained in the hands of the thieves.

These stories are full of specialist language that people outside the industry struggle to understand.

So if you're unsure what the blockchain or a crypto echange or even a cryptocurrency itself are, here are some key terms and what they mean.

While many may struggle with the finer points of crypto, pretty much everyone has heard of its most famous product: Bitcoin. But what actually is it?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is to say a type of digital currency. Unlike traditional currencies, Bitcoin is not controlled by centralised financial institutions.

This makes it popular for people who think decentralisation can bring financial freedom, but it also makes it extremely volatile with it rising and falling in value at the whim of Bitcoin buyers and sellers.

Donald Trump has pledged to make the US the "crypto capital of the world" - backtracking on his previous claim that Bitcoin was a "scam".

Its price topped a much-awaited threshold of $100,000 in December 2024, then rose to $120,000 in July 2025 as US politicians prepared to debate bills to regulate digital assets.

In October 2025, Bitcoin hit an all-time high of around $126,000, buoyed by a continued wave of institutional investment and positive market sentiment. But it has been known to plummet in value just as quickly as it spikes.

In early February 2026, its price dipped below $65,000 to effectively wipe out gains achieved under President Trump.

Against the backdrop of these frequent price fluctuations, speculation continues about the true identity of Bitcoin's mysterious inventor known only as Satoshi Nakamoto.

Blockchain is the technology underpinning all cryptocurrencies, and many related products like non-fungible tokens (NFTs). In essence, it is a virtual spreadsheet on which all the buying and selling of crypto is recorded. They are arranged in blocks linked together in a giant chain - hence the name.

Every cryptocurrency transaction is individually recorded onto the blockchain by a huge network of volunteers verifying its authenticity by using computer programmes.

The incentive to do this for Bitcoin's network is that the first person to validate transactions is rewarded in Bitcoin. This potentially lucrative process, known as mining, is also controversial because of the incredible amount of energy, external used as people the world over race to be the first to successfully update the blockchain.

ETFs are portfolios that let investors bet on multiple assets without having to buy any themselves. Traded on stock exchanges like shares, their value depends on how the overall portfolio performs in real time. They can comprise a combination of gold and silver bullion, for example, or a mix of shares in both technology and insurance companies.

A spot Bitcoin ETF buys the cryptocurrency directly, "on the spot", at its current price, throughout the day.

While some ETFs already contained Bitcoin indirectly, the US approved several spot Bitcoin ETFs in January 2024. This allowed new investors, such as investment management firms like Blackrock and Fidelity, to enter the speculative world of Bitcoin without having to worry about digital wallets or navigating crypto exchanges.

XRP is a cryptocurrency used by a platform called the XRP Ledger. It was created by the co-founders of financial services company Ripple Labs in 2012 as a cheaper, faster alternative to Bitcoin.

The cryptocurrency has a fixed supply of 100 billion coins, which were created when it launched. Much of it is held by Ripple and periodically released into circulation.

Unlike cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, transactions made using XRP are verified through consensus - whereby the majority of validators on its peer-to-peer network must agree whether or not a transaction is valid before it is added to its blockchain.

This has been credited with allowing many transactions to take place simultaneously, at high speed and low cost - making it appealing to financial institutions or for processes like cross-border payments. But as with other cryptocurrencies, XRP has received regulatory scrutiny and seen sudden, sharp declines in value.

Sports.title: Ciara Mageean: European champion and Olympian dies aged 34
Sports.text:
Former European champion and two-time Olympian Ciara Mageean has died at the age of 34.

Mageean, from Portaferry in Northern Ireland, was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer in May 2025.

She represented Ireland at the 2016 and 2020 Olympics, but was forced to withdraw from the 2024 Paris Games because of an Achilles injury.

Earlier in 2024, Mageean had clinched the first major title of her career when she took 1500m gold at the European Championships in Rome.

Prior to that she had also represented Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, winning 1500m silver at Birmingham 2022.

A statement posted on her social media on Sunday said: "At 6.30am this morning, Ciara lost her battle with cancer surrounded by her loved ones.

"A beloved daughter, sister, wife, friend and inspiration to so many, she will be deeply missed.

"Ar dheis Dé go raibh a hanam (may her soul rest in peace)."

In a statement on social media, Athletics Ireland said: "We are heartbroken. An inspiration to so many, Ciara will be remembered for her courage, kindness and incredible spirit.

"Our deepest sympathies are with her family, friends and loved ones at this difficult time. Rest in peace, Ciara."

In October, Mageean wed her long-term partner Thomas Moran in a small civil ceremony in Belfast.

A talented athlete from a young age, Mageean played camogie for Portaferry GAC, but her dream of representing Ireland at the Olympics led her to pursue a career in athletics.

Her running prowess was clear during an impressive junior career that yielded 1500m silvers at the 2010 World Junior Championships and 2011 European Junior Championships. She also reached the 2010 Commonwealth Games 1500m final as an 18-year-old.

However, Mageean's early progress in the senior ranks was hampered by a serious ankle injury, which ended her hopes of making her Olympic debut at London 2012.

Having had surgery in 2013, Mageean won the Irish 1500m title on her return in July 2014.

In 2016, she claimed 1500m bronze at the European Championships in Amsterdam, but her Olympic debut ended in disappointment as she exited the 1500m competition at the semi-final stage.

In late 2017, Mageean left her Dublin base to join Steve Vernon's Team New Balance in Manchester after parting ways with coach Jerry Kiernan.

And while she endured some disappointing results following the move, Mageean claimed a European Indoor bronze medal in March 2019 before clocking two minutes 31.06 seconds to take 3.6 seconds off Sonia O'Sullivan's 27-year-old Irish 1,000m record at the 2020 Diamond League Monaco meet.

Sports.title: East Carolina Pirates' David Coleman Jr suffers fractured leg after slip by referee
Sports.text:
A referee accidentally fractured a college football player's leg during a bizarre incident in the first half of East Carolina Pirates' win against Temple Owls.

East Carolina defensive back David Coleman Jr was standing on the field with team-mates in between plays, when an official ran in to address something near the 40-yard line.

As the official approached the players from behind, he slipped and slid into Coleman Jr, who fell forward to the ground.

Coleman Jr stayed on the turf, before eventually being helped from the field by two team members, who carried him so he did not have to put weight on his injured leg.

East Carolina coach Blake Harrell later confirmed Coleman Jr had an X-ray at half-time which showed he fractured his fibula during the incident.

"Our thoughts and our prayers are with him. But that's just one of those things. Kind of wild it happens, I'd never seen that from an official," said Blake.

East Carolina won the game 17-9, with Coleman Jr recording one tackle during the match before he left the field.

Sports.title: How Harriet Dart revived career under former Wimbledon champion Marion Bartoli
Sports.text:
In the hour following her first WTA title win, Britain's Harriet Dart had little time to respond to the stream of congratulatory messages flashing up on her phone.

Most pressing was making a call to her proud parents, Nick and Susie, who had been watching the final with friends at their local tennis club in north London, and her sister Phoebe.

The next person she spoke to was 2013 Wimbledon champion Marion Bartoli.

Dart has been coached by the French former world number seven since the start of the season on a part-time basis, and she credits Bartoli for helping her achieve what some thought was beyond her.

On Sunday, with Bartoli watching from home, the world number 115 won the Guangzhou Open in China by beating rising Austrian teenager Lilli Tagger.

"It's been quite incredible to work with Marion, and I was really fortunate she was open to working with me," Dart, 30, told BBC Sport in a video call from Guangzhou.

"I'm obviously at a very different stage of my career to someone who is, say, 20. But I still feel I have a lot to improve and there are gains to be made.

"She really believes in me - that means the world to me. Seeing a Grand Slam champion having that belief has made me believe a lot more in myself."

When Dart started working with Bartoli, she was ranked outside the top 160. The pair live close to each other in Dubai and spend training blocks together there when Dart is not on the road.

Dart and Bartoli, who has a young family, are not travelling full-time together on tour, but there have been opportunities for them to work on the ground, particularly during this year's Grand Slam tournaments.

Dart says 42-year-old Bartoli still hitting the ball "really well" in practice is another benefit of the partnership.

In Guangzhou, Dart was accompanied by her fitness trainer Dario Gonfiantini and boyfriend Stephen Falck. Without her coach, Dart had to largely rely on figuring things out herself - with the help of Bartoli sending over observational notes.

Dart is projected to rise to 83rd on Monday after lifting the Guangzhou trophy to cap a stunning second half of the season.

Dart has won 19 of her 24 tour-level matches on the hard courts since Wimbledon, taking her overall record on the WTA Tour this season to 23 victories from 34 matches - the highest winning percentage of her career.

"More than anything, Marion is just a great person. She cares about me as a person first and foremost, as well as improving me as a tennis player, of course," Dart said.

"It's been invaluable and amazing for her to share her experiences to make me better.

"I've learned a lot from her and look forward to continuing to learn more. I hope we will be able to spend more weeks together next year."

Dart reached a career high of 70th in the world in 2024, having made the Wimbledon third round and US Open second round, but has languished outside the top 100 for most of the past two seasons.

During this period there have been clear vulnerabilities with her game, with opponents learning they could take advantage of a slow second serve that tended to produce double faults.

There have also been questions about her on-court mentality and whether she could handle the pressure moments.

In Guangzhou, she answered those doubts with a series of gutsy wins where she needed to fight back from behind.

"She's always had a fantastic work ethic and has always set the bar high with her professionalism," Anne Keothavong, Britain's women's team captain, told BBC Sport.

"But there is certainly more belief and confidence now. She's in a very good place.

"She's been grinding away on the tour for a long time and it's great to see someone who has put in a lot of time to succeed and win a big title."

Keothavong named Dart in her squad for September's Billie Jean King Cup Finals and although she did not select Dart to play in the tie, she was impressed by her ball-striking during practice.

Taking that level back on tour has helped Dart continue what has been an encouraging few weeks for British women in the Asian hard-court swing.

Sonay Kartal reached the final of a WTA 1000 event in Wuhan, Katie Boulter made the semi-finals at a WTA 250 in Osaka and now Dart has won her maiden title at WTA 250 level.

Last week, teenager Hannah Klugman won the biggest title of her career at the Wrexham Open - a W100 event on the second-tier Challenger tour.

"The way they're all performing towards the end of the season - at whatever level - has been impressive," added Keothavong.

"It's not easy at this time of the season because there has been a lot of tennis played, but they've all capitalised and risen to the occasion.

"It's great reward for all their hard work and is encouraging for British tennis."

Sports.title: Women's Super League: Defeat for London City - but is Europe a real possibility?
Sports.text:
It shows how quickly London City Lionesses have progressed that they were hugely disappointed with a narrow defeat by defending champions Manchester City.

For a team that were playing second-tier football 18 months ago, their lofty ambitions of qualifying for the Champions League suddenly don't seem farfetched.

London City looked like the better team for most of the afternoon at Hayes Lane but were given a harsh lesson by the visitors in how to be ruthless.

Manchester City needed goals from Khadija Shaw and Lauren Hemp against the run of play, but they dug in to win 2-1 and to continue setting the pace at the top.

Those goals came after countless opportunities went begging for London City, who ended the game having had 24 shots but only six on target.

The performance was enough, however, to show that London City are more than capable of competing with the WSL's elite.

The next question, is whether they can do it consistently.

London City Lionesses are a club who do things differently and, backed by US billionaire Michele Kang, they are not shy to disrupt the current order.

They are an independent women's football club who have spent big in the transfer window and agreed a record-breaking shirt deal with Nike believed to be worth more than £3m a year.

They have built their own training facility in Kent and persuaded superstars such as Alexia Putellas to join in the summer.

Spain international Putellas showcased her latest Ballon d'Or trophy - the third of her career - before kick-off on Sunday.

London City Lionesses are clearly no minnows, but even a squad full of superstars needs time to gel.

It was for this reason that people doubted whether they were ready this season to qualify for the Champions League and break the WSL's traditional top three.

But on Sunday's showing, they are not as far off as people thought.

Manager Eder Maestre said the team's performances are already at the level they want but results have not always shown that and they still have work to do.

"That's why it's a very frustrating situation. We were speaking a lot about respecting the identity and it doesn't matter the team that we were facing," the Spaniard said.

"The next step in that project was showing everybody that we can perform, while respecting that identity that we are trying to build on.

"That's why it's doubly frustrating, because I think the result was not the one we deserve. Manchester City are more mature.

"They are more used to it. When you have this consistency and you are very used to playing these kinds of games, maybe you have more experience.

"That's why we have extra nervousness in the moments that we need to be more clinical."

Where London City fell was where Manchester City stood tall.

Moments of brilliance by world-class players Shaw and Hemp delivered the goods and when London City's pressure grew, so too did Manchester City's resilience.

It is that consistency across 90 minutes, and the season as a whole, that Manchester City manager Andree Jeglertz believes will demonstrate the difference.

"They are a very good team and they really showed the highest level," said Jeglertz.

"What it means to be at the top of this league, is playing week after week, and at the same level - and finding different levels to win.

"That is what we have created. That's what everybody who wants to win something needs to be able to do. To contest, you need to compete for the whole season."

London City Lionesses are providing plenty of optimism on the pitch but even if they were to qualify for the Champions League this season, are they allowed to?

Current Uefa rules state that owners cannot have two clubs competing in the same competition meaning one of Kang's Lyon or London City Lionesses would miss out.

It is a dilemma that many have discussed but if they continue to perform so well, it could prove to be a problem earlier than expected.

"First of all, what we feel is important, is to be part of the conversation," London City's chief executive officer Martin Semmens told BBC Sport.

"The next stage is getting towards trophies. Our ambition is to be in Europe, to play in Europe every year, and to compete with the likes of Barcelona and Arsenal.

"We're probably one step behind that in squad development and all the other things we have to do. But on our day, we feel we can beat them."

London City's ambitions are clear - so what happens if they do qualify this season?

"I think Michele [Kang] has a really clear view and that is that she wants to see as much investment come into the women's game as possible," added Semmens.

"The men's multi-club ownership rules is about being careful not to have control over two clubs. We see it differently on the women's side.

"We want to see more investment, so we believe if you invest in more than one club, the game will accelerate faster.

"We truly understand and respect the rules, always. But there are logical, structured ways that we can compete in Europe next season."

For a team that were playing second-tier football 18 months ago, their lofty ambitions of qualifying for the Champions League suddenly don't seem farfetched....

Sports.title: Rugby League World Cup: How England plan to avoid repeat of early exit
Sports.text:
The time for excuses is over - and those in charge of English rugby league know it.

There were mitigating circumstances behind England's early departures from the Men's and Women's Rugby League World Cups.

But there is also an acknowledgement within the Rugby Football League that, for both the men and the women, a group-stage exit is just not good enough.

Within minutes of the men's exit being confirmed on Sunday morning as Tonga defeated Samoa 20-18 in an epic, the RFL had announced a plan to map out the future of the English game.

Former Great Britain men's captain Paul Sculthorpe, retiring England women's skipper Jodie Cunningham and international great Adrian Morley will be among those helping to put together that plan.

The RFL has promised more names will be confirmed on the panel in the coming days - to build on work started earlier in the year under a scheme it is calling One Game, One England.

Its aims - to build a system that develops players from grassroots and academy level who will ultimately be good enough for the international stage - chime with the recent words of Brian McDermott, head coach of England's men's team.

McDermott has spoken more than once during this World Cup campaign about the need to strengthen the structures of the English domestic game in order to give the national team a fighting chance.

And while England were not helped by their travel schedule, or a group format that effectively meant they were facing elimination from the moment they lost their opening match to Tonga, or injuries that robbed them of key players, they will not pretend that all is fine.

Ian Nolan, the RFL's new chief executive, has made clear that he recognises that.

"There are plenty of mitigating reasons why we failed to reach the knockout stages, many of which were out of our control, such as travel itineraries and format of the competition, but we can't use these as excuses," Nolan said.

"Likewise, we were also criticised for what happened with the TV rights and the tournament going behind a paywall [on Premier Sports]. We had no control over who the rights were sold to. However, television is an important element of capturing the imagination of the next generation.

"This analysis of our national game will be all-encompassing, including how we can influence media rights, balancing reach and revenue, and attracting new audiences.

"But on the pitch, we must look at why we have consistently struggled to make our mark on the world stage for more than half a century; this isn't just a recent problem."

England's women have not been helped by the fact they are playing in a domestic competition - the Women's Super League - that is effectively amateur, while being asked to compete at a World Cup against professionals from Australia's NRL Women's Premiership.

But they do have a development programme in place - the Diploma in Sporting Excellence (DiSE) is designed to bring through young female players, in years 12 and 13 of the education system, who have the potential to play at the elite level.

"Grassroots investment in our women and girls' game only started a few years ago," Nolan said. "We've started that journey.

"Stuart Barrow took a very young side to this World Cup, with 11 graduates from our DiSE programme. We're very much building for the next World Cups – the average age of our squad was just 21 years old - but the groundwork is starting to pay off."

England's exit from the Men's Rugby League World Cup was confirmed on Sunday, exactly 12 months to the day after their Rugby League Ashes challenge officially ended.

On 1 November last year, Australia won 14-4 in the second Test at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium to secure a series victory.

That defeat, and the one that followed in the third Test at Headingley seven days later, set in motion the chain of events that led to Shaun Wane's departure as head coach. He left in January and McDermott arrived in April.

McDermott - with no mid-season international or warm-up matches to fine-tune a style of play - has produced improvements.

England were good in patches against Tonga, were as ruthless as they needed to be against France, and were doing everything required of them for the opening 20 minutes against Papua New Guinea before losing their way completely.

McDermott wants to stay on for the 2030 World Cup and, given the right preparation time, could well bring further progress.

He is, however, fighting with one hand tied behind his back.

Australia's NRL is king in the rugby league universe: the seven-year, A$5.3bn (£2.78bn) television contract it signed in July is evidence of that. The three-match State of Origin series, staged in June and July, dominates the calendar at the point Europe might try to squeeze in an international window.

It means that if England want to play the southern hemisphere sides - as they must in order to keep improving - they can only do so in October and November, and even then must work around the southern hemisphere's Pacific Championships.

That makes it even more important that English domestic rugby league finds a way to bridge the quality gap between itself and the Australian game - to ensure Super League players are facing the best week in, week out.

The NRL's ongoing negotiations to invest in Super League may help. Peter V'landys - chairman of the Australian Rugby League Commission, the NRL's parent body - remains keen to do a deal despite a struggle to reach agreement.

"I think there's some dominoes could start falling our way if the NRL invests and we accept their investment," McDermott said just under two weeks ago.

But as he has also pointed out, the problems in English rugby league are too deep to be solved quickly with financial investment.

"New South Wales clubs have got about six teams [from youth level up to the senior side]," McDermott said last month. "And every one of those teams have got a six [stand-off], a seven [scrum-half] and a nine [hooker] and a one [full-back]. And they all play consistently.

"Super League clubs... I don't think they could populate three teams underneath them with a genuine six, seven, nine and one [the spine of the team].

"And this is not a new opinion, this has been going on for a long time.

"It's nothing to do with professionalism. It's nothing to do with commitment. It's nothing to do with good quality coaching or commitment from players. It's just the size of the competitions."

What is clear is whatever the future for English rugby league, there are no quick fixes, even with the One Game, One England panel in place.

As Nolan puts it: "The panel will help us form some big decisions and changes. Those decisions might need the support of the entire game, and progress won't be achieved overnight. These will be changes that pay off in four, eight, 10 years' time."

Sports.title: Qatar MotoGP: Yamaha withdraw from race - could there be implications for Formula 1?
Sports.text:
Japanese MotoGP team Yamaha have withdrawn from the Qatar Grand Prix because of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

The event at the Lusail International Circuit is set to take place on 6-8 November, having been postponed from April.

MotoGP is going ahead with the race, despite reports 19 of 22 riders have signed a letter raising concerns, external about competing in Qatar during the US-Israeli war on Iran.

In February, the United States and Israel launched air strikes against Iran, which in return fired missiles at Israel, and at other countries in the region with links to the US.

Yamaha said it has "not identified sufficient grounds to change its existing company-wide travel restrictions" on travelling to the Middle East, with the Japanese government advising its citizens against non-essential travel to the region.

MotoGP said it is "disappointed" by Yamaha's decision, which it says does not reflect the "extensive assurances" it has been given by Qatar and independent safety advisors that the race can go ahead.

Qatar has said it can guarantee teams would not be stranded in case of any escalation in the conflict.

How Israel resolves its political deadlock following recent elections and the results of Tuesday's US midterms could have significant impacts on the situation in the Middle East.

MotoGP added there will be "sporting implications" for Yamaha's withdrawal. Fellow Japanese outfit Honda and Yamaha's satellite team Pramac Racing are currently set to compete in Qatar.

Sports.title: ‘We have effing unbreakable love’: how the maverick Natalie Nakase led the Valkyries to WNBA glory
Sports.text:
The mighty, miserly Golden State Valkyries won their first WNBA title on Saturday night with a point guard Dallas had given up on and cast aside, a starting forward who had been waived five times and a late-blooming All-Star once passed over by every team in the league. That made them a fitting match for their coach. Natalie Nakase has pieced together a basketball life on making small openings count, turning a walk-on place at UCLA into a scholarship and an unsolicited scouting report into a coaching job in Japan’s top men’s league.

The Valkyries’ nerve-shredding 68-63 fightback over the Atlanta Dream in Game 7 did more than make them the fastest expansion team in major North American professional sports history to win a championship – as 45-1 preseason longshots in their second season of existence. It was proof of concept for an organization that gave overlooked players the resources, responsibility and trust to become champions – and enlisted a leader whose own circuitous journey had taught her what those things could unlock.

“We have unconditional love that’s fucking unbreakable, guys,” a keyed-up Nakase said during the trophy ceremony at a Chase Center that remained packed to the rafters, where Golden State’s 53rd home game had delivered their 53rd sellout crowd on a night that will be long remembered in the Bay Area as Ballhallaween.

“This is for all the people that have been underrated, misunderstood,” she said. “This is for all y’all, because this is proof: if you put all your heart and all your soul, you fucking win championships!”

From the first game in franchise history to a title in 534 days: the speed was extraordinary but the foundation was deliberate. Golden State had built a place where players could expect investment, opportunity and the trust of their coach – and were expected to give something back. The 46-year-old Nakase’s declaration of love came with demanding basketball obligations: defend, compete and accept whatever role helped the team win.

Veronica Burton, their starting point guard, had been waived by the Dallas Wings two years earlier, returning home to work out at the West Suburban YMCA in Newton, Massachusetts, with her high school coach while waiting for another chance. Connecticut signed her, then left her unprotected in the expansion draft. With Golden State, she became the league’s most improved player.

Kaila Charles had been cut five times in five seasons. Back at her parents’ home, training with her brother and mulling her professional future, she was preparing to visit Trinidad for her grandmother’s 94th birthday when the Valkyries offered a seven-day hardship contract. Now she was starting in the WNBA finals.

Kayla Thornton went undrafted, was shown the door by two different teams and spent years establishing herself as a dependable supporting player before becoming a first-time All-Star with Golden State at 32. Cecilia Zandalasini had started only six WNBA games before joining the Valkyries and starting 44 across the team’s first two seasons. Kaitlyn Chen, a relatively unheralded third-round draft pick, found a role backing up Burton and as the bench’s chief vibes officer. Tiffany Hayes, a former sixth woman of the year, had played more WNBA games without winning a title than anyone else in history – until Saturday night.

These were careers transformed by opportunity – by a team willing to explore what its players could become. Gabby Williams, the newly minted WNBA finals MVP and Golden State’s closest thing to an incandescent star, put it another way.

“All it took was good people,” Williams said. “All we heard last year was we don’t have no stars. We don’t have no talent. Yeah, right! We got good people. We got good people. We got winners. We got people who are ready to put their bodies on the floor to win a game.”

Nakase understood what it meant to have more to offer than others could see. She had spent much of her own career proving it.

A 5ft 2in point guard from a basketball-obsessed Japanese-American family in southern California, she turned down a scholarship to UC Irvine to walk on at UCLA, her dream school. A torn ACL delayed her start, but she earned a scholarship there anyway, became a starter and captained the Bruins for three seasons.

She never did make a WNBA roster. Phoenix cut her in 2007, before another knee injury while playing in Germany spelled the end of her playing career. She began coaching the Wolfenbüttel Wildcats of the Damen-Basketball-Bundesliga before moving to Japan, where she initially found a foothold watching Tokyo Apache practices. A scouting report she prepared earned her a volunteer assistant’s job under former NBA coach Bob Hill, before she eventually became the first woman to lead a team in Japan’s top professional men’s league when she took charge of the Saitama Broncos.

Then came a return to California and an internship in the Los Angeles Clippers’ video department. She spent a decade in the organization, working through video, development and coaching roles before Becky Hammon brought her to Las Vegas in 2022. Two championships as a bench coach followed, giving her a front-row seat for one of basketball’s great dynasties.

Her intensity can work against her. Nakase nearly fainted in the closing minute of the first-round decider against Dallas, prompting her to pay closer attention to rest, hydration and nutrition. During the semi-finals, she took the unusual step of giving herself a full day off. The coach who constantly urged her players to “empty the tank” had run up against her own limits. Nakase traced both that relentless drive and her instinct to invest in people to her late father.

“He’s the reason why I’m built the way I am. I am crazy. I am obsessive. I am a workaholic,” she said. “But it’s more just pouring into people, believing in people, helping people, that’s all come from my dad.”

Her extended apprenticeship mattered for a roster assembled largely from other franchises’ spare parts. Nakase and general manager Ohemaa Nyanin looked for competitiveness and character, studying even how players behaved when they returned to the bench. They needed people who wanted more for themselves and could still accept what the team required.

They worked at those relationships. On an early two-week road trip, the Valkyries organized dinners and games built around open, honest questions. Basketball, Nakase said, was the last thing they wanted to discuss.

“I love to learn about people, so I can push their buttons and go crazy when I have to,” she said.

Williams remembered evenings nobody wanted to end. “I knew we had something special on that trip.”

“Strength in numbers” was one of Nakase’s recurring messages, alongside “Empty the tank”. She backed it with her rotations, sometimes trusting the eighth or ninth player to finish games. Shared responsibility gave Golden State the depth to sustain their suffocating defense – the best in the league by some distance – and made a larger role a real possibility for everyone on the active roster. That extended to closing an elimination game with a rookie (Chen) while her starting point guard (Burton) watched from the bench. Opportunity depended on what the game demanded, while established players had to trust that the same principle applied to everyone.

The finals tested that bargain. Trailing Atlanta 2-1, Nakase moved Charles and Tiffany Hayes into the starting lineup, bringing Thornton and Zandalasini off the bench. Golden State won the next two games, holding Atlanta to 62 and 55 points. Trust had a practical application: players could lose their starting places without the team losing them.

There was individual greatness, too. Williams poured in 28 of her 30 points after half-time in Saturday’s deciding game, the highest-scoring half in WNBA playoff history, and was the no-brainer pick for MVP. Her explanation began with her coach.

“Nat told me to stay patient. I trust her with my life,” Williams said.

Williams had taken her own peripatetic journey to the summit, building a decorated career in Europe and with France while her WNBA progress came in interrupted stretches in Chicago and Seattle. “I may have done things the hard way, took my own route, but I loved it,” she said. “It built character, it built me into the person I am, and it landed me here. It landed me with the best group of people I’ve ever been around.”

The newly minted finals MVP explained Saturday what made Golden State different. “I showed up new to the team, the team already had a culture and relationships established but I walked into a group full of love and that just changed the entire trajectory of my career,” she said.

The conditions for all this mattered. Nakase linked up with an owner whose impatience matched her own and whose ambitions came with a pledge to provide the resources needed to fulfill them. Joe Lacob’s requirement during her interview was straightforward: whoever took the job had to win a championship within five years.

“I’m impatient,” Nakase said after delivering it in two. “I’m obsessive but it’s because he pushes me.”

She spoke, too, about the value of Lacob’s presence, of an owner who kept showing up throughout the playoffs. His investment gave the expectation substance. “Someone who invests in women’s sports,” she said, “this is a result.”

As the curtain falls on the WNBA’s milestone 30th season, the pattern is becoming impossible to miss. Las Vegas paid Hammon $1m a year to leave the NBA and constructed a $40m training facility, backing a championship core with the infrastructure to flourish. New York’s revival began when Joe and Clara Wu Tsai rescued the Liberty from willful neglect in Westchester, moved them to Brooklyn and invested in everything from recruitment to nutrition. Golden State have followed the same principle: invest deeply in the conditions for success, then demand it.

Money alone cannot create the trust that lets a coach change her starting lineup midway through the finals, but culture needs material backing. Players notice the quality of their facilities, the support around them and whether ownership’s ambitions extend beyond a speech. Increasingly, the WNBA’s championship race is being shaped by which organizations understand that connection. Golden State’s achievement is the most accelerated demonstration yet.

And this is hardly an exercise in altruism. The Valkyries recently became the first women’s professional sports team to exceed $100m in annual revenue, according to Sportico. The demand was reflected on the secondary market: Game 7’s cheapest available ticket was $364 roughly 24 hours before tipoff, outstripping every NFL and college football game this weekend, according to ticketing analyst Keith Smith. Turns out taking women’s basketball seriously is good business.

Lacob’s own accounting of the championship began with three women: Nakase, Nyanin and team president Jess Smith. “Those three women made this happen,” he said during Saturday’s trophy ceremony, before turning his thanks to the supporters who had embraced the franchise before it had a single player – and filled the 18,064-capacity arena in Mission Bay to capacity one night after another.

The culture belonged to that whole enterprise. Ownership supplied resources and expectations. The front office identified players hungry for responsibility. The coach created space for them to grow while demanding they make room for one another. The fans gave a new franchise an immediate sense of belonging. In the end Nakase was uniquely suite to connect those ambitions. She had spent her career asking people to look beyond the obvious credentials, then rewarding their faith with the work. She recognized that same hunger in the players Golden State brought together and it’s paid off faster than anyone could imagine.

The result was a championship in 534 days, built by people who knew how long a chance could take to come.

Sports.title: Liverpool v Arsenal: Premier League – live
Sports.text:
51 min We’ve carried on where we left off, Liverpool again peppering the Arsenal box with crosses, again to little avail. Oh but this is better, Nyoni punching into Mac Allister, who turns to Isak, who flicks around the corner for Kerkez … who’s offside. Nevertheless, those are the kind of moves Liverpool need to construct, one-touch passing against which Arsenal’s defence can’t set.

49 min Thinking again about Jasper’s email, the point with Isak isn’t so much about him taking a dive, but making enough of a confident fuss to make sure VAR take a serious look.

48 min Araujo, of whom we’ve seen relatively little, crosses, but the various attackers are on their heels.

46 min Has Arteta made any tactical tweaks, or will he just have instructed his team to show a little more composure in possession? It may be that his attackers just aren’t good enough to take the ball and attack defenders one on one; dare he gamble on Eze, who has form for carrying it on this grounf?

46 min We go again…

“I really dread the suggestion that Isak ‘should have made more’ of the pull on his shirt,” says Jasper Walgrave. “It’s a clear penalty for all to see and there’s VAR. Saying players should make a whole scene for a clear penalty to be awarded is throwing bait at all the divers and the fakers and the theatrics which we should so love to get rid of.”

Yes, I agree, but if VAR can’t be trusted, what are players to do? I think there’s also a problem inherent within the laws and spirit of the game: some fouls are tolerated because we want a contact sport that flows, in which goals are earned. So stuff is let go as “not enough for a penalty” though, according to the letter of the legislation, there’s no doubt.

Half-time email: “Re the top of the PL, I agree,” says Tim Stappard. “Considering the billions spaffed the quality is very poor. Who has a great defence a great midfield and a great attack in this league?”

And how many attackers are top five in the world? Not many. As I intimate below, winning the league is always an achievement and the money in it means the teams from sixth to 17th had never been better. But the standard was relatively low, though the physicality was extremely high.

Half-time reading:

It’s the way I tell em.

HALF-TIME: Liverpool 0-1 Arsenal

A bouncing half of Premier League FootballTM, throbbing with tempo and burgeoning needle, if lacking a bit of composure and quality. It was excellent fare and Arsenal lead thanks to a decent start and superb Declan Rice cross. But there’s much, much more to come.

45+2 min Barcola stretches, ploughs Timber thigh to thigh, and the ref decides that is where he’s drawing the line; booking. Which is was yet, at the same time, it makes no sense given what was waved through earlier in the half.

45+1 min We’ll have two additional minutes.

45 min “Arsenal fans are well used to being told that our title was won by default,” chortles Christian Gunn, “that refs gave it to us, unworthy champions, Set-Piece FC etc but ‘absence of high class challengers’ is a fruity new one! And entirely fictional! Please critique as much as you like but at least keep it on the straight and narrow. Anything else? Your mate saw Ben White drowning kittens? Martin Zubimendi puts forks in the spoon bit?”

You think the standard at the top of the Prem is high? The Champions League suggests otherwise, and so does the eye-test. A title is a title and none are to be sneezed at, but I’d be shocked to hear anyone rhapsodise the quality at the top.

42 min Liverpool have Arsenal serried in their box once again, but another cross is cleared and off we go again. I’m surprised this is how they’re trying to score because of how well we know Gabriel, Calafiori and Konsa defend them but here they go yet again, Kerkez bouncing down the left and Mac Allister arriving on the burst; ye’ve gottae score! But though he introduces brow to ball, he sends it over the top, to receive instant appraisal from a sensitive soul in the away end.

Updated at 12.34 EST

39 min It’s Wirtz who unleashes a dipper that soars over Raya … and cannons the bar! That was a terrific effort, but Liverpool have got to make their pressure count before Arsenal get to reorganise at half-time. This is, by some distance, the best Premier League game I’ve seen this season.

Updated at 12.24 EST

38 min Liverpool win a corner Gabriel is certain they shouldn’t have, then Isak beats Madueke only to be tackled by Timber. The ref, though, appraises a foul; free-kick just outside the box, left-hand side, Wirtz and Gakpo behind it.

36 min Mac Allister opts not to shoot left-footed having opened the lane, so plays into the box and when the ball squirts off Barcola, Isak takes a touch before shooting wide of the near post. Arsenal, meantime, lack an out-ball and are also struggling to play out.

34 min We’re shown the 20th-minute cross on to which Isak couldn’t stick a head, and Timber has a proper handful of his shirt. In co-comms, Gary Nevile can’t understand why he didn’t make more of a fuss and he’s right – unlike the Tzoils/Gakpo one, that was enough for a penalty.

33 min I’m enjoying Liverpool’s breathless onslaught, but I’d like to see a little more finesse – of thought was well as of action. They’re putting Arsenal under pressure with speed and territory, but aren’t asking questions by getting them turned and chasing runners; more take-ons and quicker combinations are required.

31 min Yet another ball into the box and Kerkez appears at centre-forward, but he can’t quite get away from Konsa.

29 min Another ball lofted into the box, Gakpo chasing and Tzolis sort of holds him, then he hurls himself into the turf knowing he’s not getting it. On the touchline, Iraola, is certain it’s a penalty, but though VAR takes a look this is never getting overturned, nor should it be.

Updated at 12.02 EST

28 min Liverpool are putting ball after ball into the box but if there’s one thing these Arsenal defenders know how to do and there isn’t, there’s more, it’s clear their lines.

27 min Goodness, there’s some tempo to this now, Calafiori fouling Gakpo; again there’s no carde and the ref has set a standard of permitted foul now. The free-kick causes minor panic and earns a corner, headed on by Van Dijk, Raya doing enough to block Isak’s touch when he sneaks in behind.

Updated at 12.13 EST

25 min The problem Liverpool have is that as they chase an equaliser, they leave themselves vulnerable to conceding a second and, as I type, Tozlis curls to the back post and Madueke is there, extending a leg to divert the ball back across. But just as it looks headed for Havertz, it hits Timber then, seconds later, Rice hammers a shot straight at Alisson.

24 min Mac Allister lasers a ball left to Kerkez, who does well to keep it in but then crosses straight to a defender. So Arsenal move down the other end, Madueke option not to attack Kerkez, instead siding backwards to Bruno, who sweeps into the middle; the ball kicks off Van Dijk’s shin and flies behind, but the ref doesn’t spot the deflection.

22 min Liverpool come again, Gakpo mooching over to the left and sliding in behind for Barcola, who might cut back first time but instead opts to wait, giving the defenders enough time to block the various passing lanes.

20 min Liverpool have been better since falling behind and Wirtz finds Barcola, who steps inside to swing in a brute of a cross, just too much on it for Isak ... who may have been tugged back. But they come again, Arsenal giving it away and Barcola speeding by Rice on the outside, his low cross intercepted by 176 defenders sliding in to put faces in the way if need be. That’s why they’re champions.

Updated at 12.30 EST

18 min Back come Liverpool, stung. Raya passes out poorly and Barcola seizes the loose ball, but there’s Rice, arriving out of nowhere to make the challenge. In terms of ability, he’s not the greatest around, but his intangibles – desire, nous, leadership, consistency – are top notch.

GOAL! Liverpool 0-1 Arsenal (Havertz 16)

A poor pass-out from Alisson puts Liverpool under pressure and Odegaard is first into press, the ball squirting oose. Quickly, Arsenal move it right, Bruno and Tzolis involved, then Rice storms around the outside of Madueke, fed the ball into stride before measuring a perfect cross through the corridor, Havertz running it in at the far post.

Updated at 12.24 EST

14 min Arsenal are starting to dominate in midfield, but do they have enough attacking edge to create? Their trio is an attacker short, I think, and I wonder if they might find better chemistry with Guimaraes seeking to control so Rice can gambol forward. Oh, and as I type, they do just that, Rice thwacking high.

13 min “Just because Arteta’s paranoid, doesn’t mean his team didn’t weren’t pipped to first three years running by a club conspiring against the league,” writes Kári Tulinius. “However, because of his personal employment history, he can’t bring that up, and instead talks like the relative you least want to be seated next to at the holiday dinner.”

I’m not sure how much fun he’d be even in different circumstances.

10 min A poor touch from Nyoni, who chases it and this time, introduces studs to heel, Havertz down. Somehow, he once again avoids a booking when really, he’s doing well to still be on the pitch; the first one was a stonewaller and the second wasn’t far off it, while I’ve not a clue how the combination of the two lead to no sanction.

Updated at 11.43 EST

9 min Timber clips a long pass in behind for Havertz but Liverpool catch him offside – not necessarily because theirs is a well-drilled offside trap.

8 min This time, Wirtz pinches possession deep inside his own half and finds Isaka, who punches a pass through the middle for Barcola, one of those speedsters who looks like a flying cartoon character. But Raya is wise to the ruse, racing out to hump clear.

Oh but this is better, Nyoni punching into Mac Allister, who turns to Isak, who flicks around the corner for Kerkez … who’s offside. Nevertheless, those are the kind of moves Liverpool need to...

Gaming_Tech.title: US tech stocks see sharp falls as AI spending nears $1tn
Gaming_Tech.text:
Tech stocks tumbled for the second day in a row as concerns rise over the hundreds of billions of dollars firms are investing in artificial intelligence (AI).

Shares in Intel plummeted by 28% on Friday, while Google owner Alphabet saw its stock price continue to fall another 1.4% after a 12% plunge on Thursday.

Other tech stocks, including Reddit and Amazon also fell, while the Nasdaq index of the largest tech firms listed in the US, ended October with its worst monthly slide since March 2025.

While tech firms are spending big on AI, their earnings are not always meeting analysts' expectations, spooking investors and creating fears of an AI bubble.

Major tech companies have ramped up artificial intelligence spending, with Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft committing to spending $800bn between them in 2026.

Alphabet's stock market value fell sharply on Thursday, taking more than $500bn (£374bn) off its market value after it revealed the AI summaries it now provides as the top answer to search queries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.

At the same time, Alphabet expects to spend up to $205bn this year on investments, almost entirely related to AI.

The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere however, with Intel shedding more than $130bn in value.

The chip maker said it planned to increase spending on AI despite weaker demand for computers, a major source of demand for its micro-processors.

On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.

"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.

In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.

Amazon on Thursday revealed it had also spent more cash than it was making, and that spending had increased six-fold over the span of three months.

The company has committed to spending $220bn this year, putting the money towards investments such as AI data centres, network equipment, and servers.

Amazon shares recovered some overnight losses, but were still down by 1.4% at the end of Friday trading.

Reddit stock plunged by 29%, after the social media platform revealed weaker-than-expected daily user figures and warned that Google's growing AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic.

Stock in online game platform Roblox also fell, down by 18%, as its daily active user numbers dropped.

Several major tech firms have reported earnings this week, including Microsoft, and analysts said there were questions about the payout from the huge investments in AI.

Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google.

He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out".

"The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."

Gaming_Tech.title: Neoclouds: These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst
Gaming_Tech.text:
A once-obscure corner of the AI ecosystem finds itself in the spotlight – and investors don't all like what they see.

Names like CoreWeave and Nebius are familiar to the tech set in San Francisco and Silicon Valley.

These data centre companies, known as neocloud firms, run large warehouses packed with expensive computers, which they lease to major AI developers like Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta.

They're now the subject of one of Silicon Valley's most heated debates.

Many question whether neocloud firms are financially sound and what their recent stumbles tell us about the state of the AI economy.

Analysts at Gartner predict by 2030, 80% of neocloud firms will "cease independent operations", while Forrester's experts expect at least three of them to be imminently acquired "as finances get shaky".

On Thursday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent tried to downplay recent concerns about neocloud firms, calling them "a small component of the overall ecosystem, external" on CNBC.

Neocloud firms often finance themselves by signing long-term lease contracts with major tech customers who need quick access to computing power.

Firms can then borrow money using those contracts – plus the AI chips they purchase – as collateral, explained analyst Cory Johnson of "The Quiet Period" IPO research outfit.

He said debt is common across neocloud firms because the hardware has to be paid for up front.

Take the industry leader: CoreWeave. It's a fraction of the size of some of the Big Tech companies it serves.

But Johnson believes lenders sometimes consider the creditworthiness of CoreWeave's customers, like Microsoft or Meta, more than the company's when they lend.

"This helps explain how CoreWeave accumulated $35.1bn (£26.3bn) in debt," he said.

Some jittery investors appear to be having second thoughts.

CoreWeave stock has lost a quarter of its value over the past month, and it's not alone.

Shares in other neocloud firms like Nebius, IREN, and Applied Digital have all shed about that much if not more during the same period.

Debt investors also appear spooked, and are demanding ever-higher returns from several firms in the sector.

CoreWeave's CEO Mike Intrator has said that the market is acting "irrationally" and has expressed confidence in its business model. Some of the world's most consequential companies are queuing up for CoreWeave's infrastructure and other AI services.

Several neocloud firms have their roots in the volatile crypto mining industry, made of companies that generate cryptocurrencies, like Bitcoin.

Crypto miners use some of the same kind of physical infrastructure that is used to develop AI.

CoreWeave was founded in 2017 with a focus on mining Ethereum.

IREN, Core Scientific and Applied Digital also started in crypto mining.

Their infrastructure left them well-positioned when AI exploded in 2022 with the introduction of OpenAI's ChatGPT.

One outlier is Nebius, which was known as Yandex NV when it was part of Russia's version of Google before splitting off and changing its name in 2024.

Now, the success of these firms hinges on the fate of major AI developers and hyperscalers – even larger data centre operators which neocloud firms often count as key customers.

"There is just an enormous amount of spending getting injected into the system," said Melissa Otto, head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global. "It's an arms race."

And neoclouds have benefitted.

But the trade-off of their model is "greater financial risk" in the face of change, said Forrester VP and principal analyst Charlie Dai.

That includes any adjustments that their Big Tech customers might make to their spending plans.

This past week, when Microsoft and Google forecast less AI spending than Wall Street analysts had projected, shares in several neocloud firms tumbled.

Much is also riding on Anthropic and OpenAI, which are both expected to start selling shares to the public in the months ahead.

If AI proves to be a bubble – and bursts – neocloud firms "are definitely going to face collateral damage," said Bradley Tusk of Tusk Ventures.

Gaming_Tech.title: Google value plunges by $500bn as its own AI search hits ad sales
Gaming_Tech.text:
Google-owner Alphabet lost just over $500bn (£374bn) in value on Thursday after it revealed its own artificial intelligence (AI) summaries were hitting search advertising revenue.

Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said Google's "AI mode", where it answers questions conversationally, was eating into the money it makes from ads which appear next to results to traditional search questions.

Yet, Schindler said he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine.

Google's role in answering the world's questions has been challenged by the AI boom, with millions of people using programs such as ChatGPT and Claude instead.

Kim Scott, who formerly led Google's advertising business, told the BBC's Today programme that the company would "rather eat its own lunch than allow someone else to eat their lunch" by having its own AI summaries hit its search revenue.

She said that Google was founded on the idea of making long-term bets on technology – even if they hurt the firm in the short term.

"I think they're making a long-term bet on AI," she said.

In its results published on Wednesday, Alphabet revealed that total revenue grew 25% in the three months to the end of September, compared to the same period last year, hitting $127.6bn.

However, the firm did not make as much money as analysts had predicted, particularly in its advertising arm, which spooked many investors.

Shares in the company plummeted over 12% to a six-month low following the release of the results.

By the end of Thursday, the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before.

Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing Search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses."

Microsoft and Amazon also issued updates this week, and joined Google in plans to keep spending huge sums of cash in the ongoing AI race.

But investors appeared dismayed at the impacts these plans are having on the ability of each to keep growing their core lines of business.

Amazon's stock took a hit on Thursday , with its shares falling 6% in after-hours trading.

Alongside quarterly sales growth of 11%, hitting $201bn, the company shared a staggering cash flow figure of negative $42bn.

That number shows that Amazon is not only spending more money than it makes, but that spending has increased six-fold over the span of three months.

Chief executive Andy Jassy claimed the business was spending in part because it had the chance at, not one, but two businesses that could end up bringing in $1 trillion for Amazon the future.

Jassy noted that Amazon's cloud services business, as well as retail stores, may be those businesses. During a call with financial analysts he also repeatedly mentioned the financial opportunity presented by Amazon making and selling its own computer chips, as well as its AI developer platform Bedrock, which offers paying users access to most major AI models and tools.

"One of the lessons we've learned over 20-plus years is that there is not one tool to rule the world," Jassy said. "People always assume whatever is in the lead early on will be the only thing that people use - it's never true."

As Jassy was asked several times to explain the company's spending, he admitted it "would be more convenient" if it were spread over the next 25 years. "That's not the world we live in," he added.

"We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size, the revenue, the free cash flow of Amazon."

Gaming_Tech.title: Crypto giant Binance hit by hack suspected to be largest in history
Gaming_Tech.text:
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that $6.3bn (£4.7bn) of digital assets have been impacted by what is thought to be the biggest crypto hack on record.

The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses".

The firm said while initial checks suggested an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, "our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach".

Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor.

Cyber-security firm Check Point said the unit is also known in the industry as Lazarus Group, which has been blamed for the 2025 hack.

Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record".

AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.

The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen.

The attacker still holds an enormous sum of stolen assets, meaning efforts to trace and recover the funds are far from over, Redbord added.

Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.

The company said in 2024 that it has more than $160bn in assets under its custody.

The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.

Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack.

For the last few years North Korea-linked operatives have focussed on attacking cryptocurrency companies for large thefts of digital tokens.

Western security agencies have previously said stolen funds are used to finance North Korea's nuclear weapons and missile development programs.

The regime has denied any involvement in hacks in the past.

Eric Jardine, Chainalysis' Head of Research, urged every exchange to remain vigilant as the platforms are attractive targets for hackers due to the sheer value of assets.

Binance did not directly respond to BBC questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice."

The incident concerns Binance.com - while much smaller crypto platform Binance.US, which provides trading services specifically for American residents - said its platform is not affected by the issue.

Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the company's initial investigation suggested the hack started with a compromised engineer's laptop.

"That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions," he said in a statement.

"To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual. So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak."

He said a detailed "post-mortem" would be shared once the investigation was complete.

In an update, the company said in a statement on X that another investigation found there had been other breach points: "We are still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them."

Check Point's Dave said this attack also resembled a hack on crypto exchange platform Bitget in September in which $388m (£289m) was lost: "This implies that attackers no longer need the vault keys. They target the systems and people with authority to use them."

In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets.

"Safety first: withdrawals are currently disabled until the environment is confirmed to be secure," she said.

Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they had frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack.

World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said it has worked with its partners to freeze stolen funds.

Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation.

Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue.

Bitcoin dropped by more than 4% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply.

Gaming_Tech.title: How video game remakes tap the power of nostalgia
Gaming_Tech.text:
The moment she saw footage from the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, Kacey Doran picked up her phone. She had to tell her sister.

"Have you seen this?" messaged Doran, excitedly.

Nearly 30 years ago, a 10-year-old Doran had sat in front of her family's TV, reading out the dialogue on screen to her sister, a year younger, as they inched their way through the original Nintendo 64 game's sprawling, puzzle-filled dungeons. Ocarina's fantasy-like story, and beautiful music, enthralled them both.

It was also the first game Doran ever completed. Now, countless memories rushed back to her as she devoured clips of the fully redesigned version, due to arrive on the Switch 2 later this year.

Doran's sister messaged back: "I'm not tearing up… YOU'RE tearing up."

This is the power of nostalgia – and a perfect example of how video games can trigger it. Doran now teaches an esports course at Rowan University in New Jersey. She says the original Ocarina of Time, released in 1998, had a "magical" quality that she hopes to rediscover, and also share with her sister's children.

The video games industry has long leaned on remakes. From Mario Kart to the Final Fantasy series, or even Pac-Man, some games just keep coming back in updated forms, as new generations of gamers emerge and as computer hardware improves, enabling more detailed graphics and increasingly expansive game worlds.

While the emotional hook may be the most significant draw, putting out a remake can be a double-edged sword. Some gamers are very protective of their favourite titles and new versions don't always meet certain fans' astronomically high expectations.

Nostalgia is an important but mixed emotion, says Tim Wulf, at the Centre for Advanced Internet Studies in Bochum, Germany. It has positive aspects but also a kind of sadness, too. Happiness in remembering things that were important to us, and also an awareness that that time is now gone.

"It's a social emotion because memories that induce nostalgia for us are connected to other people," he explains, adding that nostalgia can boost our self-esteem while highlighting key social bonds.

Video games, says Wulf, are notoriously good at triggering nostalgia because gamers can "jump into the same environment". In other words, games are like time machines for our emotions, and returning to fondly remembered places can feel stabilising or reassuring in an ever-changing world.

Doran, for one, notes that when you return to a favourite old game, there's something satisfying about deploying previously learned skills. You know what to do here, you're winning again. Just like the old days.

Putting out remasters and remakes has been a "really successful" strategy for the games industry, says Piers Harding-Rolls, head of games research at Ampere Analysis.

"Tying in with established audiences and building on existing content is quite a safe route for a lot of companies," he adds. In many cases, it is cheaper to update an existing game rather than create a new title from scratch.

Among other remakes that have found big audiences recently are those of Resident Evil 4 and Assassin's Creed Black Flag.

But Ocarina of Time perhaps stands out because, ever since its original release, it has been considered by many as one of the greatest games ever made. "The interest from all the Gen Zs that I work with is really high," says Harding-Rolls. The legend of The Legend of Zelda, as it were.

Clearly, nostalgia is not the only driver of interest in the remake, and today's audiences will expect a game that plays to today's standards.

Games companies must keep innovating when linking contemporary audiences to the past, says Wulf, in order satisfy their desire for fresh experiences. And although Wulf himself was a big fan of the original, he has no personal interest in the Ocarina of Time remake. "I want a new game – I don't want to play an old game," he says. Nostalgia isn't always enough for some.

Plus, critics often highlight a tension between originals and remakes. Which is the definitive version? In 2021, Square Enix released the bizarrely titled Nier Replicant ver.1.22474487139... – a remaster of a game first published in 2010. One reviewer wrote, external, "What we're left with is two nearly identical Niers each vying to be the true Nier."

Fans may react badly should a remaster or remake fail to do justice to the source material. And, in the gaming world, angry fan reactions can be serious.

"There's always going to be that fan base or group of people that are going to nit-pick," says Stephanie Ijoma, chief executive and founder of NNESAGA, a consultancy and creative agency.

Ultimately, games developers working on remakes have to "find the right balance" between appealing to fans and allowing themselves to be creative with the material, she adds. "You can't make art in fear, you can't create in fear."

Ijoma gives the example of Final Fantasy VII. First released in 1997, it got a highly anticipated remake in 2020.

This was a game Ijoma played back in the late 1990s and she was thrilled to be able to share it with younger players today.

Remakes enable this sharing of experiences because getting old computer hardware or video games consoles to work, while a pastime loved by some, is not possible for everyone.

"I've tried multiple times to play Silent Hill 2 because I'm interested in older games but it's such a difficult game to come into nowadays," says Niklas Hallin, a solo indie game developer who runs the studio Neckbolt. "They made a remake and it's so smooth, it just works. It works on your modern hardware."

Hallin did not play many games as a child so he says nostalgia isn't much of a motivator for him. However, in his own games, he likes to include subtle stylistic references to classic games because he knows that this appeals to gamers.

Indie developers often lean on retro games aesthetics not just because people respond well to them – but also because they are easier to achieve. "You can't compete with billion dollar budgets, super high-fidelity, Triple A graphics," he says.

One question remains. The visual difference, today, between games released years apart is, arguably, negligible. So will there be any point in remaking a game from 2026 in, say, 2038? Will technology have moved on so much by then that it's actually worth it?

Harding-Rolls predicts that games companies will still seek to connect new audiences with classic titles by offering updates.

Remakes might become less about graphical improvements and more about editorial adjustments. "Reinterpretations," he says. "Or versions with additional content."

It's never really "game over", is it?

Gaming_Tech.title: Ofcom outlines age verification for under-16s ahead of social media ban
Gaming_Tech.text:
Ofcom has set out its recommendations for the most effective ways to identify which of the UK's millions of social media users are aged over 16.

Under the UK's social media ban - which is due to come into force in March next year - those under that age will be prevented from accessing ten of the biggest platforms, including Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.

Many UK adults are also likely to have to confirm that they are not under-age by using one of the proposed measures, which are subject to government approval.

A similar ban was introduced in Australia last year but many children there have found ways to get round it. The UK says it intends to take a tougher approach.

Age verification below 18 is challenging because 16 and 17 year olds don't have credit cards or full driving licences, and may not have passports either. They can also look significantly older or younger than they are.

To address that challenge, Ofcom has - in addition to traditional forms of ID - recommended four methods that it says would be "highly effective" at gauging people's ages:

photo ID matching, where relevant information on a photo ID document such as a passport is checked against a live image taken during an age check

banking-based checks, which involves using the information a financial institution has on record regarding a user's age

face age estimation technology (which the regulator argues has recently improved)

digital ID services, which enable people to digitally prove who they are or provide information about themselves, such as their age

The BBC has asked three of the UK's biggest banks whether they would have a process for assisting with social media requests for age verification if it did become an official measure.

However, ultimately it will be up to the tech companies to figure out how to implement the checks: the onus is on social network providers to come up with their own solutions and comply.

Ofcom CEO Dame Melanie Dawes said the regulator was drawing on its experience in introducing tougher age checks for porn sites last year:

"What we've learned in introducing age checks across the porn industry is that actually what a lot of countries did before us was say you need to do it this way and they were very prescriptive and it didn't work," she told the BBC.

"So what we've said all along is here are things that can work, they must preserve privacy, they must protect people's data, but it's on you to put in place what you think works for you."

Some of the tech companies, including Meta, have called for age verification to be applied at device level, so that someone under-age would be automatically blocked from installing social media apps via app stores.

Meta told the BBC it already applies some methods recommended by Ofcom to enforce its user age requirements or place users in Teen Accounts settings.

But it said applying age checks at device-level, via app stores, could reduce the burden on people to have to repeatedly verify their age across multiple platforms.

This would place responsibility with Apple and Google, who between them operate most of the world's smartphones. Apple has already introduced age verification in the UK.

However Ofcom says that would not absolve the social network providers from doing their own checks as well.

The regulator said it didn't have a firm number for how many adults would need to prove they were not under age, but conceded that it would be a "large number of accounts" that social media companies would need to "deal with."

It has also acknowledged that "the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated", and some children would succeed in bypassing the age checks.

Dawes said making the ban work would be a joint effort.

"At Ofcom, what we will do is make sure that the services that the social media companies put in the checks that they need to," she told BBC News.

"That's our job, but the wider question about how everybody engages with this, it is for everybody, really.

"I actually think the real prize here is going to be for today's eight to 10-year-olds entering secondary school without it being the norm to go on Snap in your class group chat, without it being the norm to have all your sports fixtures organised on Instagram."

Ofcom's age verification report will now be considered by the government, with a decision due by the end of the year.
